captions.text: A palindrome reads the same from either end.
Matching digits sit in paired places on either side
of its centre.
A repunit is made entirely of ones.
Place value lets us build a repeated digit
with one multiplication.
In AMC Upper Primary practice, watch for numbers that
read the same when reversed, or a long row
of repeated digits.
In a Rossmoyne style puzzle, add a divisibility rule.
Use the mirror structure to leave fewer free choices.
Take the repunit one hundred and eleven and
multiply by three.
What number will you get?
Picture multiplying each place separately.
Look for any place that would need a carry.
Each one becomes a three.
The product in every column is below ten, so no digit
has to move into the next place.
The answer is three hundred and thirty-three.
You can view it as one copy of that digit
in every position.
The four-digit number two thousand seven hundred and
seventy-two reads the same both ways.
Divide it by eleven.
Can you find the quotient by splitting the outer and
inner pairs of digits?
The two outer copies of two contribute two
thousand and two.
The two inner copies of seven contribute seven
hundred and seventy.
One thousand and one is eleven times ninety-one.
One hundred and ten is eleven times ten.
Both pairs share a factor of eleven.
Now add ninety-one times two and ten times seven.
The quotient is two hundred and fifty-two.
Count the five-digit palindromes divisible by nine whose
first digit is at most nine.
The first and last digits match.
So do the second and fourth.
The centre can be any single digit allowed by
the divisibility test.
A five-digit palindrome is fixed once we choose its
first two digits and the centre.
Call them A, B and C.
The digit sum is twice A plus twice B plus C.
For each outer pair choose C to make the sum a
multiple of nine.
There is always a choice from zero through eight,
since those digits give all nine remainders.
Nine is a second choice precisely when
zero already worked.
That happens when A plus B is itself divisible by nine.
The pair can sum to nine, with one partner from zero to
eight for each allowed first digit.
The pair nine and nine also sums to eighteen.
Add ninety and ten.
The answer is one hundred, with each number counted once
by its three free positions.
Starting with zero would give fewer than
five written digits.
Only the centre and the second digit may start from zero
in this count.
When the required remainder is zero, both zero and nine
work as centre digits.
Test those two endpoints before you count.
Write only the independent digits first.
Use the mirror pairs to copy the other positions.
Use the divisibility test on the resulting digit sum.
Check whether the residue allows two single digits.
